'''''Hydrangea quercifolia''''', commonly known as '''oakleaf hydrangea''' or '''oak-leaved hydrangea''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Hydrangeaceae]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Hydrangea quercifolia - Plant Finder | url = https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286892&isprofile=1&basic=hydrangea%20quercifolia|access-date=2021-03-02|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> It is [[native plant|native]] to the southeastern United States, in woodland habitats from [[North Carolina]] west to [[Tennessee]], and south to [[Florida]] and [[Eastern Texas]].<ref name="lbjwc">{{Cite web|website=Plant Database|publisher=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=HYQU3|access-date=11 March 2023|title=''Hydrangea quercifolia''|author=TWC Staff|date=18 October 2022}}</ref>  A [[deciduous]] shrub with white showy flower heads, it is grown as a garden plant, with numerous [[cultivar]]s available commercially.

Its [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] combines the [[Latin]] words {{Lang|la|quercus}} ("oak") and {{Lang|la|folium}} ("leaf"). However, it is not closely related to oak species (''Quercus'').

==Description==
''Hydrangea quercifolia'' is a coarse-textured [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] growing to {{convert|3 - 12|ft|m}}<ref name="lbjwc"/> tall with an open crown. The plant sprouts shoots from underground [[stolons]] and often grows in colonies. Young stems are covered in a felt-like light brown bark, and the larger stems have attractive cinnamon-tan-orange [[Bark (botany)|bark]] that shreds and peels in thin flakes.

The [[leaves]] are yellowish green to dark green on top and silvery-white underneath. They have three, five or seven pointed [[Lobe (anatomy)|lobes]] and are 4–12 in (10.2–30.5 cm) long and almost as wide. They vaguely resemble larger versions of oak leaves, similar to ''[[Quercus]]'' species with lobed foliage. Plants in shade have larger leaves than those grown in sun. The leaves turn rich shades of red, bronze and purple in autumn that persist in winter accompanying the persistent dried flower-heads.

===Flowers===
''Hydrangea quercifolia'' flowers are borne in erect [[panicles]] 6–12 in (15.2–30.5 cm) tall and 3–5 in (7.6–12.7 cm) wide at branch tips. Flowers age in colour from creamy white, aging to pink and by autumn and winter are a dry, papery rusty-brown.

Unlike [[Hydrangea macrophylla|bigleaf hydrangea (''Hydrangea macrophylla'')]], flower color does not vary with [[soil pH]]. Flower color does, however, vary throughout each growing season. The flowers are a pale green as they emerge and open to a bright white, ageing to either pink or brown (depending on the cultivar/seedling).<ref name=":1" />

''Hydrangea quercifolia'' and ''[[Hydrangea paniculata]]'' are the only hydrangeas with cone-shaped flower clusters (i.e. [[panicle]]s); all the others have their flowers in ball-shaped or flat-topped clusters, called [[umbel]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.floridata.com/ref/H/hydran_q.cfm|website = Floridata|title=#52 ''Hydrangea quercifolia''|access-date=11 March 2023}}</ref>

Like many other ''[[Hydrangea]]'' species, oakleaf hydrangea [[inflorescence]]s are composed of two flower types; showy flowers with enlarged petal-like [[sepal]]s and inconspicuous flowers with non-showy petals and sepals.<ref name=":1" /> The showy flowers, whose function is to attract pollinators, typically obscure the inconspicuous flowers to some degree.

Although faint, ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' flowers have a pleasing scent. The [[floral scent]] in oakleaf hydrangea is stronger than that of the other commonly cultivated ''Hydrangea'' species.<ref name=":1" /> Presumably the function of the floral scent is to attract pollinators, although this has not yet been studied. The fragrance can be described as being most similar to [[Syringa reticulata|''Syringa reticulata'' (Japanese tree lilac)]], although not as strong.

=== Fruit ===
The fruit of ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' are [[Capsule (fruit)|dry dehiscent capsules]] which are green following [[pollination]] and ripen to brown as they mature. The [[Floral morphology|stigmas]] remain on the fruit and dry to form horn-shaped appendages atop the capsule with an opening between them to allow the seeds to [[Seed dispersal|disperse]].<ref name=":1" />

=== Seeds ===
''Hydrangea quercifolia'' [[seed]]s are quite small, approximately 0.6 mm long<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hufford |first=Larry |date=1995 |title=Seed Morphology of Hydrangeaceae and Its Phylogenetic Implications |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/297279 |journal=International Journal of Plant Sciences |language=en |volume=156 |issue=4 |pages=555–580 |doi=10.1086/297279 |s2cid=85030866 |issn=1058-5893|url-access=subscription }}</ref> (and with a thousand seed weight of 0.0356 g<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Seed Information Database |url=https://ser-sid.org/species/2edc5770-354c-4262-8319-7008dc5937b3 |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=ser-sid.org}}</ref>) allowing several to develop within each capsule. Seed color varies from light tan to dark brown with longitudinal striations. Seed shape is ellipsoidal to ovate. [[Seed bank|Seed storage]] behavior is considered to be [[Orthodox seed|orthodox]] in nature,<ref name=":2" /> allowing them to store for relatively long periods of time at cold temperatures. The seeds typically [[germinate]] readily in 7–14 days as long as they are not allowed to dry out after sowing.

==Distribution==
''Hydrangea quercifolia'' is native to the south eastern United States (Alabama, Florida, Georgia (w.), Louisiana (e.), Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee), but naturalized in other parts of the US and widely cultivated elsewhere.

In nature, ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' is found in a variety of [[habitat]]s but almost always on well drained, shady slopes. These include riverbanks, bluffs and rocky outcroppings. The tendency of the species to grow on [[calcareous soils]] or cliffs as well as deep [[alluvial soil]] suggests it has a wide tolerance of soil substrates as long as they are well drained.<ref name=":3"/><ref name=":1">{{Citation |last1=Sherwood |first1=Andrew |chapter=Oakleaf Hydrangea ( Hydrangeaquercifolia Bartr.): Horticulture, Genetics, Breeding, and Conservation |date=2022-02-03 |chapter-url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781119851981.ch1 |title=Horticultural Reviews |pages=1–33 |editor-last=Warrington |editor-first=Ian |access-date=2023-11-22 |edition=1 |publisher=Wiley |language=en |doi=10.1002/9781119851981.ch1 |isbn=978-1-119-85195-0 |last2=Clark |first2=Matthew D. |last3=Hokanson |first3=Stan C.|s2cid=243795333 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Uses==
[[Image:Hydrangea quercifolia4normanack.jpg|thumb]]

===Garden history===
''Hydrangea quercifolia'' was noted by 18th-century botanist [[William Bartram]] in his botanizing exploration from the Carolinas to the Florida panhandle in the 1770s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.arhomeandgarden.org/plantoftheweek/articles/Oakleaf_Hydrangea.asp|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050315191804/http://www.arhomeandgarden.org/plantoftheweek/articles/Oakleaf_Hydrangea.asp|archive-date=15 March 2005|date=26 March 1999|website=Arkansas Home & Garden|publisher=University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service|title=Plant of the Week: Oakleaf Hydrangea}}</ref> His first documentation of the plant was located along the "brook called Sweet Water" in what is now south-central Georgia.<ref>William Bartram, [https://www.loc.gov/resource/rbctos.2017gen02676/?sp=7&st=image "Travels through North & South Carolina, Georgia, East & West Florida, the Cherokee Country, the extensive territories of the Muscogulges, or Creek Confederacy, and the country of the Chactaws; containing an account of the soil and natural productions of those regions, together with observations on the manners of the Indians"] (1791), James & Johnson, Philadelphia.</ref> It was slow to enter British and American gardens. In Britain it flowers less profusely and even has a reputation for being tender.<ref>Alice Coats, ''Garden Shrubs and Their Histories'' (1964) 1992, ''s.v.'' "Hydrangea".</ref>

===Cultivation===
''Hydrangea quercifolia'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] in gardens and parks. Though frequently seen as an isolated subject in gardens, it is at its best in a natural or landscaped woodland habitat against the backdrop of larger shrubs and trees. It prefers partial to almost full shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade as optimal. It will tolerate drought, but may not flower. In the UK the [[cultivar]]s {{tdes|'''Snowflake'''}}='Brido'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/218386/i-Hydrangea-quercifolia-i-Font-Face-times-New-Roman-Snowflake-FONT-Brido-(d)/Details | title = ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' {{tdes|Snowflake}}='Brido' | access-date = 11 March 2023|website=RHS Plantfinder|publisher=The Royal Horticultural Society|year=2023}}</ref> and {{tdes|'''Snow Queen'''}}='Flemygea'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/139947/i-Hydrangea-quercifolia-i-Font-Face-times-New-Roman-Snow-Queen-FONT-Flemygea/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' {{tdes|Snow Queen}}='Flemygea' | access-date = 7 March 2018}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 51 | publisher = The Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 3 March 2018}}</ref>

Propagation is via cutting or division; short sections of clustered stems with some root attached will make a small shrub in a nursery row.

Fresh or dry, the blossoms of ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' are attractive as cut flowers.

==== Cold hardiness ====
Oakleaf hydrangea is typically stated to be hardy to [https://planthardiness.ars.usda.gov/ USDA Zone 5-9],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hydrangea quercifolia (Oak Leaf Hydrangea, Oakleaf Hydrangea) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/hydrangea-quercifolia/ |access-date=2021-03-02 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> although the true cold hardiness varies for each cultivar and throughout the [[species range]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Sherwood |first1=Andrew |last2=Alexander |first2=Lisa W. |last3=Clark |first3=Matthew D. |last4=McNamara |first4=Steve |last5=Hokanson |first5=Stan C. |date=2021-09-01 |title=Horticultural Characterization of Wild Hydrangea quercifolia Seedlings Collected Throughout the Species Native Range |url=https://journals.ashs.org/hortsci/view/journals/hortsci/56/9/article-p1023.xml |journal=HortScience |language=en-US |volume=56 |issue=9 |pages=1023–1033 |doi=10.21273/HORTSCI15889-21 |issn=0018-5345|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dirr, Lindstrom, Lewandsowski, Vehr |date=1993 |title=Cold Hardiness Estimates of Woody Taxa From Cultivated and Wild Collections |url=https://meridian.allenpress.com/jeh/article/11/4/200/79270/Cold-Hardiness-Estimates-of-Woody-Taxa-From |access-date=2023-11-29 |journal=Journal of Environmental Horticulture |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=200–203 |doi=10.24266/0738-2898-11.4.200|doi-access=free }}</ref> Plants from more northern sources are typically [[Cline (biology)|more cold hardy]] in midwinter than plants from southern sources; moreover, plants native to Florida are substantially less cold hardy than those from other southern sources.<ref name=":4" /> Cold hardiness also varies throughout winter, with early loss of cold hardiness being the main limiting factor to cultivation in northern environments. The cultivar 'Ruby Slippers' maintains its cold hardiness well into April, while 'Sikes Dwarf' (despite being very cold hardy in midwinter) loses its cold hardiness very rapidly in late winter. Out of nine cultivars tested, {{tdes|'''Snow Queen'''}}='Flemygea' was consistently the least cold hardy throughout winter.<ref name=":4" />

==== Diseases ====
There are several notable diseases that infect ''Hydrangea quercifolia''. [[Root rot|Root rot diseases]] can be fatal<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Baysal-Gurel |first1=Fulya |last2=Kabir |first2=Niamul |last3=Blalock |first3=Adam |date=2016-01-01 |title=Root Diseases of Hydrangea |url=https://digitalscholarship.tnstate.edu/extension/140 |journal=Tennessee State University Extension Publications}}</ref> while [[foliar disease]]s tend to be only cosmetic.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Baysal-Gurel, Kabir, Blalock |date=2016 |title=Foliar Diseases of Hydrangeas |url=https://www.tnstate.edu/extension/documents/Foliar%20diseases%20of%20Hydrangea%20FBG%20022916%20G1.pdf |journal=Tennessee State University Extension Publications}}</ref> Root rot diseases include ''[[Phytophthora]]'', ''[[Pythium]]'' and ''[[Fusarium]]'', which are all [[fungal diseases]].<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Neupane |first1=Sandhya |last2=Alexander |first2=Lisa |last3=Baysal-Gurel |first3=Fulya |date=2023-07-01 |title=Evaluation of Hydrangea Cultivars for Tolerance Against Root Rot Caused by Fusarium oxysporum |url=https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-11-22-2712-RE |journal=Plant Disease |language=en |doi=10.1094/PDIS-11-22-2712-RE |pmid=37392028 |s2cid=259303524 |issn=0191-2917|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Integrated pest management|Management techniques]] to decreases [[Incidence (epidemiology)|incidence]] of root rot include proper watering (allowing the soil to dry between waterings), removal of diseased plant parts, and fungicides if needed. Compared to other ''Hydrangea'' species, oakleaf hydrangea is more susceptible to ''Fusarium'' root rot; however, disease severity varies among cultivars with 'John Wayne' and {{tdes|'''Snowflake'''}}='Brido' being the most tolerant.<ref name=":7" /> The primary foliar disease in oakleaf hydrangea is ''[[Xanthomonas]]'' leaf spot, which is a [[bacterial disease]].<ref name=":6" /> Management techniques to decrease leaf spot severity include avoiding overhead irrigation and planting [[resistant cultivar]]s. In a recent study, the cultivars 'Alice' and {{tdes|'''Snow Queen'''}}='Flemygea' had the lowest disease severity while 'Queen of Hearts' had the highest severity.<ref name=":4" /> Some wild plants that are native to Florida have even lower disease severity than any cultivar and could serve as an important seed source for breeding disease resistance.<ref name=":4" />

== Genomics ==
Oakleaf hydrangea is a [[diploid]] species with 2n=2x=36 [[chromosome]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van Laere |first1=K. |last2=Van Huylenbroeck |first2=J. |last3=Van Bockstaele |first3=E. |date=2008 |title=Karyotype analysis and physical mapping of 45S rRNA genes in Hydrangea species by fluorescence in situ hybridization |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1439-0523.2007.01456.x |journal=Plant Breeding |language=en |volume=127 |issue=3 |pages=301–307 |doi=10.1111/j.1439-0523.2007.01456.x |issn=0179-9541|url-access=subscription }}</ref> ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' has one of the [[Genome size|smallest genomes]] in the genus (1.95 - 2.17 pg 2C DNA).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cerbah |first1=M. |last2=Mortreau |first2=E. |last3=Brown |first3=S. |last4=Siljak-Yakovlev |first4=S. |last5=Bertrand |first5=H. |last6=Lambert |first6=C. |date=2001-07-01 |title=Genome size variation and species relationships in the genus Hydrangea |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s001220000529 |journal=Theoretical and Applied Genetics |language=en |volume=103 |issue=1 |pages=45–51 |doi=10.1007/s001220000529 |s2cid=6690336 |issn=1432-2242|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zonneveld |first=Ben |date=2004 |title=Genome size in Hydrangea |journal=In Encyclopedia of Hydrangeas, Eds J. Van Gelderen and D. M. Van Gelderen |pages=245–251 |via=Portland, OR: Timber Press}}</ref> In nature, the [[genetic diversity]] of ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' is [[Genetic structure|structured]] geographically in six 'clusters' of genetically similar [[Population (biology)|populations]].<ref name=":3" /> These genetic clusters are weakly differentiated but each one has unique genetics nonetheless. In addition to neutral genetic diversity (13.5% of the diversity), there is evidence of genomic [[Natural selection|selection]] in response to climatic variables (11.3% of genetic diversity) of which, [[precipitation]] seems to play a major role.<ref name=":3" />

== Conservation ==
The native range of ''Hydrangea quercifolia'' appears to be contracting, despite high [[Abundance (ecology)|abundance]] in the central portion of the range.<ref name=":1" /> In a recent survey of the species, 23% of [[Herbarium|previously recorded]] [[Population (biology)|populations]] no longer existed and many of the remaining populations were at high risk of [[extirpation]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Sherwood |first1=Andrew |last2=Alexander |first2=Lisa W. |last3=Clark |first3=Matthew D. |last4=Wu |first4=Xingbo |last5=Hokanson |first5=Stan C. |date=2023-01-01 |title=Precipitation, Temperature, and Population Structure Influence Genetic Diversity of Oakleaf Hydrangea Throughout Its Native Range |url=https://journals.ashs.org/jashs/view/journals/jashs/148/1/article-p29.xml |journal=Journal of the American Society for Horticultural Science |language=EN |volume=148 |issue=1 |pages=29–41 |doi=10.21273/JASHS05255-22 |issn=2327-9788|doi-access=free }}</ref> Causes of local extirpation was attributed to [[Habitat destruction|habitat loss]] or degradation often times due to [[invasive species]], logging or commercial development. Oakleaf hydrangea was noted as not tolerating high [[Competition (biology)|competition]] and is therefore highly susceptible to the negative impacts of invasive species. The researchers noted that these effects could be mitigated by [[Protected area|protecting]] and managing land with substantial populations, especially on the species' range edge. To add to the conservation concern, many of the populations on the edge of the native range have [[Genetic structure|unique genetics]] (especially in Louisiana and Florida) making them especially important to protect as a source of valuable [[genetic diversity]].<ref name=":3" />

==Symbolism==
''Hydrangea quercifolia'' was declared the official state wildflower of [[Alabama]] in 1999.<ref>State Botanical SymbolsBy Alan McPherson, p.3</ref>
